extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, IP analysts, in-house counsel and patent owners preparing claim charts and conducting infringement analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Practical step-by-step guidance for identifying potentially infringing products and preparing tabular claim charts that map patent claim elements to product evidence for litigation or enforcement. Covers evidence types, investigation techniques, target selection, and legal doctrines (e.g., doctrine of equivalents, SEPs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of claim charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts are essential tools in patent law, particularly in cases of patent enforcement. Claim charts are a visual tool that can effectively present complex technical information clearly and concisely and significantly help to decide authorities/courts in the matters of Patent Litigation and help them understand the extent of infringement or non-infringement while studying every detail of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong claim chart is supported by expert comments from an industry expert testifying the infringement of claimed features by the infringing product. It plays a key role in the swift movement of the case and helps both the plaintiff and defendants assess their position in a Patent Litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular representation aligning claim elements to product evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim chart is a tabular representation of claimed features of a patent on one side and relevant excerpts from the product description/product features on the other side to highlight how the infringing product is infringing every claimed feature of their patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-structured claim chart requires a thorough understanding of patented technology and features of the accused potentially infringing product. Along with technical knowledge of the field of invention, a detailed understanding of marketing-related keywords is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the patented technology and define scope of claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly understand the patented technology and interpret scope of the claims using detailed description, prosecution history, and other extrinsic sources to ensure the broadest possible interpretation of claimed elements such that it covers a wide range of products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the independent claims with the broadest scope of protection and interpret the claim in a way that maximizes its coverage while staying within reasonable bounds based on the detailed description of the subject patent and the knowledge of a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify application area and product types for the patented technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the patent to understand potential fields and industries where the patent technology can be applied; use IPC/CPC class codes and cited patents to locate industry segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the technology field and products offered by companies cited in the citation list; once the application area is identified, identify types of potentially infringing products (example: Inertial Measurement Units → Mobile Phone, Smart Watch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify key companies and evaluate potential infringement targets
rubrics_metrics.description: List key players in relevant technical fields and review product specifications, industry reports and market reports to identify companies offering potentially infringing products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting a target company consider: avoid companies with existing licensing agreements or business relations with the patent owner; assess presence and revenue in the preferred jurisdiction; focus on sales and revenue of the allegedly infringing product in that jurisdiction; identify products actively sold there, launched after the patent filing date, and specific product versions that include the patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm product release after the patent priority date before detailed analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Once it is established that the identified feature/product was released after the priority date of the patent, commence a detailed analysis of the potentially infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not proceed to detailed claim charting until product timing (launch/release) is confirmed relative to the patent's priority/filing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct references as primary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncover all product-related official documents, datasheets, marketing material, video, audio, or any relevant document in any format pertaining to potentially infringing products, and released by the target company or its Executives/ Management team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully validate the authenticity of the publication source and publication dates; prioritize primary source disclosures from the company or its executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect references and inferential evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If direct disclosure of any claim element is not found, but the final or intermediate output or product feature suggests the presence of the concerned claim feature in the product, then evaluate backend logic to see if disclosed frontend features imply the use of the claimed feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support inferential claims with expert comments citing appropriate logic/arguments. Example: product documents tout a 'secure transaction' feature that—based on technical reasoning—would only be possible using the claimed encryption algorithm; highlight and substantiate this inference with expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard mapping for SEP-related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For standard essential patents (SEPs), use a two-step test to locate documents revealing use of a technical standard and map patent claims with the technical standard to establish infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, map the patent to the standard to show it is an SEP, and then show that the potentially infringing product also implements or maps to that standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source code review for computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions claiming algorithms or underlying logic in computer-related technologies, source code review can reveal the underlying algorithms and logic embedded within the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use source code review to trace data flow and operations, understand decision-making processes, and ascertain interaction of system components; particularly important where product documentation does not disclose algorithmic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teardown reports for mechanical or apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For mechanical inventions or apparatus claims, teardown reports (disassembling the device) are an effective way to determine whether a product is infringing on the patented claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismantle the device to expose independently identifiable parts for detailed analysis; teardown reveals construction and operation allowing comparison with patent claims (example: inspect hinge mechanism in a foldable smartphone to compare to a claimed hinge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering for semiconductor and fabrication-related technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: In technologies related to fabrication of semiconductor devices and processes, reverse engineering reports are effective to ascertain infringement by analyzing layered structures of a semiconductor device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse engineering semiconductor chips requires sophisticated machinery and highly skilled analytical expertise; involves deconstructing logic gates, data paths, and conducting layerwise analysis to map to claimed structures/processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents analysis when literal infringement not found
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused product/process does not literally infringe, consider whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents: does the accused product/process contain elements identical or equivalent to each claimed element of the patented invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine equivalence by analyzing the role played by each element in the context of the specific claim and assess whether a substitute element matches the function, way, and result of the claimed element or plays a substantially different role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claim chart findings with expert testimony/comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong claim chart is supported by expert comments from an industry expert testifying the infringement of claimed features by the infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experts to validate inferential evidence, explain technical mappings (e.g., backend logic, equivalence reasoning), and provide authoritative linkage between claimed elements and product evidence; explicitly cite expert logic in the chart where direct disclosures are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of marketing and domain keywords in identifying evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with technical knowledge, a detailed understanding of marketing-related keywords is essential for preparing an effective claim chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search and analyze marketing materials, product descriptions and related keywords that may reveal or imply claimed features; use these terms to locate indirect or contextual evidence and to validate product versions or features.
